episode_thesis: Mark Rzepczynski argues that the 2026 Middle East oil supply shock and the wider 'VUCA' (volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity) environment favour trend followers because supply shocks leave central banks without a clear response, so prices are free to trend, and because ambiguity makes investors slow down and spread decisions over time, producing longer trends. His research adds that managed futures returns are insensitive to VIX risk regimes and risk shocks, unlike other hedge fund strategies, which gives a diversification advantage beyond low beta though with little alpha. Niels Kaastrup-Larsen reports a strong April for CTAs, doubts that replication or extra context (AI, sentiment) improves on price-only trend following, and stresses that slower systems have done better in an era of instant information.

speakers.name: Mark Rzepczynski
speakers.role: Systematic investor and co-host of the Systematic Investor series; researcher on managed futures, replication and AI in quant investing
speakers.speaker_note: Auto-captions; stutters make some turns hard to separate. Speaker mix-ups corrected per the ledger: the UAE pipeline figures (about 1.5 million barrels a day) are his, and the 1914 reference is to the weeks after the Archduke was shot and before September 1914 (the year July 1914 is not stated).

worldview_premises.premise: The present environment is VUCA (volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity), in uncharted territory, and the practical question for a quant investor is how to navigate it.
worldview_premises.support: A theme he has raised with the host before.

worldview_premises.premise: Goldilocks condition for trend following: the longer a crisis lasts, the more time trend followers have to capture trends; short sharp crises such as March 2020, which reversed within a month, hurt them.
worldview_premises.support: 'All the research we have', no numbers; March 2020 as the example.

worldview_premises.premise: Supply shocks are harder for central banks than demand shocks (cutting rates to boost demand worsens inflation), which leaves policy unsure and prices free to trend; a persistent supply-shock inflation regime resembles the 1970s and produces extended price trends in many markets.
worldview_premises.support: Policy logic; euro-area inflation about 3% and US inflation persistently above 2% (trimmed mean).

worldview_premises.premise: Government intervention is the main risk to trends; in a supply shock the proper policy response is unclear, so prices are driven by market behaviour and not by policy.
worldview_premises.support: Argument from the contrast with recession, where policy would try to reverse a fall.

worldview_premises.premise: Governments offset the pandemic supply shock with fiscal spending, low rates and liquidity, which generated inflation and later benefitted trend followers.
worldview_premises.support: Recent history (2020-22).

worldview_premises.premise: High ambiguity and conflicting signals make investors slow down, dollar-cost average and delay action, spreading decisions over time and producing longer trends; information is abundant but human processing ability has not improved, so trends last longer than expected, favouring longer trends over a high-frequency edge.
worldview_premises.support: Behavioural reasoning; he says a direct testable hypothesis is harder to form.

worldview_premises.premise: Uncertainty indices are high but may have peaked, while VIX has declined for about eight weeks to only slightly above median, suggesting investors are numb to news. Equities holding up while an energy shock extends may mean the event is not discounted, as in the weeks before September 1914, but 'not discounted' is itself a directional opinion that needs a test.
worldview_premises.support: VIX and uncertainty index readings; one historical analogy; he admits the claim is an opinion.

worldview_premises.premise: Dislocations that extend have stronger and longer price effects: oil reversed on headlines yet stayed higher, so a trader long from early March did reasonably well despite higher volatility. Many commodities (fertilizer, propane, butane, refined products) are affected by the closed Straits of Hormuz.
worldview_premises.support: Price behaviour in March-April 2026.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend replication struggles with nonlinear, threshold-based signals (breakouts are dormant until a move passes a threshold) while moving-average strategies are easy to replicate; 'breakout' is a catch-all for threshold or trigger signalling.
worldview_premises.support: His own research experience in replication.

worldview_premises.premise: Correlation is a poor guide to replication quality: a replicator can be highly correlated yet have a negative beta to the managers it targets; the alpha not captured by simple factors cannot be replicated and is what investors pay fees for.
worldview_premises.support: Statistical argument.

worldview_premises.premise: Reverse-engineering trend programmes is not new (brokers have tried for four decades); AI is new. In the 'Mimicking Finance' study, AI agents replicate about 70% of portfolio-manager behaviour but fall short of the best managers, who are more dynamic and rule-rich; whether added complexity beats a simple replicator is an open empirical question.
worldview_premises.support: The paper; no replication of it by him.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following has near-zero equity beta and near-zero alpha in simple regressions, while other hedge fund strategies have positive beta and some significant positive alpha; trend gives diversification but little alpha.
worldview_premises.support: His simple regression of strategies on systematic risk over time.

worldview_premises.premise: Most hedge fund strategies have a negative coefficient on high-VIX risk regimes (lower excess returns when VIX is high) and their alpha turns negative in the high-VIX tercile, whereas managed futures returns are insensitive to VIX regime (coefficient not significant) and to risk shocks measured as the change in VIX; managed futures and global macro are the exceptions that do not suffer in high volatility.
worldview_premises.support: His current research across hedge fund strategies; terciles of VIX; significance tests described but no numbers given.

worldview_premises.premise: Institutional allocators choose trend following against all other hedge fund strategies that might diversify, not just against other trend followers, so its case must be made relative to the whole alternatives menu.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of allocator behaviour.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors want a story (Kahneman: 'No one ever made a decision because of a number. They need a story'), which is a constant marketing challenge for trend followers who say only 'prices go up, I buy'; managers with narrative context may win allocations.
worldview_premises.support: Two Kahneman quotes; a contrast between a trend follower and a global macro storyteller.

worldview_premises.premise: Context (NLP sentiment from earnings calls, LLMs converting non-numerical information to signals) is profitable in equities, but how to use it in trend following has not been researched; multi-agent LLM ensembles of technical, fundamental and sentiment agents show better Sharpe ratios than single agents.
worldview_premises.support: Literature he has read; 'the jury is still out' for trend.

worldview_premises.premise: Blending trend with other strategies inside one manager resembles a multi-agent ensemble; pure trend managers are becoming rarer; the open question for investors is bundle versus components, and multi-strategy platforms sell bundling hundreds of orthogonal pods with faster risk management.
worldview_premises.support: Industry observation.

worldview_premises.premise: Deep-momentum research on bimodality finds past winners split into continuing winners and big losers, which offers an explanation of momentum crashes.
worldview_premises.support: Cited research; left for a later call.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The VIX-regime and risk-shock regression results are described qualitatively; no coefficients, sample period, strategy indices or significance levels are given, so the claim that managed futures is invariant to regime cannot be checked here.
The 'Goldilocks' link between crisis length and trend returns is stated as the result of 'all the research we have' without evidence; the contrast with March 2020 is anecdotal.
Rzepczynski says a testable hypothesis for 'ambiguity favours longer trends' is hard to form, and the host's observation of slow models winning is not tied to specific numbers.
The market is 'not discounting' the shock is, by his own statement, an opinion; the 1914 analogy is a single episode and VIX behaviour has several explanations (numbness, hedging already in place).
The host's recollection that inflation hits equities with a lag is hedged ('as far as I know') and unsupported.
The 'Mimicking Finance' result (70% replication) concerns portfolio managers in general, not trend followers specifically, and she does not report how the paper measured 'behaviour'.
Ledger attribution fixes applied: UAE pipeline figures belong to Rzepczynski (C02-2) and the 1914 reference is to the weeks after the Archduke's shooting before September 1914 (C07-2).
The host reports strong 2026 returns for smaller breakout managers with static sizing but names none and gives no figures; the claim is anecdotal.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs the speakers treat as leading or diagnostic: the length of the Middle East crisis (longer lasts better for trend); oil and energy price behaviour and the Straits of Hormuz closure; persistence of inflation above 2% (euro area about 3%); the stance of the new Fed chair on the balance sheet versus rate cuts; whether government or the Fed intervenes to arrest trends; VIX level and uncertainty indices as measures of regime; CTA fixed-income positioning direction. Horizon is months for the trend, years for the regime thesis (1970s-like supply-shock inflation).
reader_inferences: (reader) Rzepczynski's argument implies a testable prediction: trend returns should be higher when crises persist beyond about a month and when policy responses are unclear, and lower for short V-shaped shocks; episodes (March 2020, April 2025, August 2024) could be classified by duration.

(reader) The 'ambiguity slows decisions' mechanism predicts positive serial correlation at longer horizons and slower systems winning when uncertainty indices are high; this could be tested against uncertainty indices.

(reader) If managed futures returns are invariant to VIX regime while other strategies lose alpha in high VIX, allocation rules that scale up trend relative to other hedge funds when VIX rises have a logical basis, but his evidence does not address the cost of waiting.
(reader) Niels's price-only view and Mark's context view are not logically exclusive: context could improve sizing or risk, not signals; neither speaker separates these uses.
